tagline.text: Beaches and gun battery ruins on a former US Army fort island at the mouth of Subic Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Subic Bay Freeport Zone, an island at the entrance of Subic Bay (reached by boat from the Waterfront Road pier)

children.text: Grande Island is a small island at the entrance of Subic Bay, once the site of the early 20th-century US Army fort known as Fort Wint. Today a resort operates it, and you can enjoy the north beach and the old battery ruins in a single day trip.
Grande Island is a small island at the mouth of the bay in the Subic Bay Freeport Zone, Zambales, Philippines. It lies about
15–30 minutes

by boat from the pier on Waterfront Road on the mainland, and its position guarding the open sea beyond the bay made it a military stronghold from the American colonial era onward. Today a private resort runs the entire island, so ordinary travelers normally get in through the resort's day tour or overnight packages.
The island's history is the history of Fort Wint. The US Army built the fort as part of the coastal defenses protecting Manila Bay and Subic Bay and completed it around
, naming it after Brigadier General Theodore J. Wint. Fourteen guns were divided among five batteries, but by the time Japan attacked the Philippines in
they were already obsolete; the fort was abandoned in
January 1942
and retaken by US forces in
March 1945
. After the war it was absorbed into the Subic Bay naval base and used as a recreation spot for service members, and in
it was the setting for Operation New Life, when thousands of South Vietnamese refugees stayed here temporarily.
After US forces left the base in

, the island reopened as a resort. Today it has manicured lawns, a shallow north beach that suits children, a large swimming pool and golf cart paths, so it draws many families on day trips. Walk into the forest, however, and you will find military remains such as concrete battery structures and a mine casemate, which means you can combine beach time and history in one visit, something that sets it apart from other beaches around Subic. After the war, the 10-inch guns of Fort Wint were shipped to Fort Casey in Washington State, while some of the 6-inch guns still remain at Battery Hall on the island. Even if you are not especially interested in military sites, climbing onto the concrete walls and gun emplacements shows at a glance why this small island was the key to the bay, and it gives families plenty to talk about with children. There are few information signs, though, so reading a short history of Fort Wint before you go will make the visit much more fun.

Keep in mind that this is not a free-to-visit public beach but a resort island you visit by reservation. Prices vary a lot depending on what is included, and on day tours the swimming pool is sometimes off limits. Before you go, we recommend contacting the resort directly to confirm the price, boat times and inclusions.

The sand beach on the north side of the island is fairly fine-grained, and the bottom deepens gradually, so swimming is easy. The sand has the slightly dark tone typical of the Zambales coast, so if you are expecting the white sand of Boracay, it will look different.

Of Fort Wint's five batteries, Battery Hall, Battery Flake and Battery Jewell were open in a 2024 visit report, and Battery Hall is reported to still have a 6-inch disappearing gun. Battery Warwick is locked because it overlaps with an airport radar installation, and Battery Woodruff has all but vanished. The batteries are large concrete structures and get very hot at midday, so go in the morning.
In the forest, the mine casemate is open and you can look inside. It is dark inside, so bring a flashlight, and some stretches are overgrown, so long pants and sturdy shoes are needed.

blocks.title: Golf cart and ATV island tour

children.text: The paths on the island have been improved and the golf cart paths widened, and carts are reported to be available for rent. Some sections have signs for ATV use, so check on site whether rentals are offered and what they cost.

There is a large swimming pool near the former Navy ball field, and the main building has a restaurant, a bar and a function room. On day tours, however, you may not be able to use the pool, so be sure to ask whether it is included when you book.

Because the island sits at the mouth of the bay, it offers views of the mountain ridges on the mainland and the boats passing by. A quiet spot on one side of the island has tree shade and is good for a peaceful rest.

The resort has offered water activities such as banana boat rides, kayaking and jet skis, as well as fishing experiences. Types and prices change from year to year, so the most reliable way is to ask at the front desk when you arrive.

items.title: Day tour
items.subtitle: From pier assembly to the afternoon return

children.text: Arrive at the Grande Island pier office on Waterfront Road in Subic, confirm your reservation and check in. According to 2024 reports, pier check-in was at 8 AM, so allow some extra time.
Take the boat across to the island. The landing has been rebuilt and sometimes uses a floating pier, so watch your footing as you step off.
Enjoy a welcome drink, get an island briefing, then swim at the north beach.
Tour Battery Hall and the old military facilities by golf cart or on foot. The forest paths are hot and buggy, so bring water and mosquito repellent.
Have lunch at the restaurant. The number of meals included varies by package.
Relax on the beach or try the water activities.
Check out from the island and return by boat. According to 2024 reports, island check-out was at 4 PM.
The schedule may be changed by the resort, so follow the information you receive when you book.

items.title: Overnight stay
items.subtitle: Evening sunset and a quiet morning

children.text: Take the boat from the pier to the island, check in and relax on the beach.
Watch the sunset on an island emptied of day visitors and have dinner at the restaurant.
Stroll the battery ruins early in the day, then return by boat in the afternoon.
From Manila to Subic (Olongapo) it usually takes about
2.5–3 hours
by car via the SCTEx expressway, and longer depending on traffic.
Buses to Olongapo and Subic run from the main terminals in Manila. Routes and fares differ by company, so check on site.
There may be a vehicle check at the entrance when you enter the Freeport Zone.
If you hire a van or use a travel agency package, you can book the Manila round trip and the boat together.
From Clark International Airport (CRK) to Subic it is about
1 hour
by car. It varies with traffic.
It is easiest to book a taxi or van from the airport.

items.title: From the pier to the island

children.text: Board the resort's own boat at the Grande Island pier (the resort office) on Waterfront Road in Subic. Sources give the crossing time as anywhere between
15–30 minutes
The boat is basically for people who have booked, so reserve in advance. The resort takes bookings by phone, email and social media.

For swimming, the dry season, when the sea is calm and the sky is clear, is best. Subic Bay is an inner bay, so the waves are relatively mild, but in the rainy season rain and strong winds can cancel boats.
On weekends and holidays the pier is crowded with families from Manila. If you want a quieter visit, we recommend going on a weekday.

To walk the forest paths or see the batteries, go in the morning before the sun climbs high. The usual order is to relax on the beach in the afternoon and return to the pier in time for the last boat.

The island has chalet-style rooms run by the resort along the shore, and the main building has a restaurant and bar. Outside food may be restricted, so check when you book. Older write-ups mention hotel-style rooms and a honeymoon suite.
Day tour packages sometimes include a welcome drink, a morning snack, lunch and an afternoon snack. If you want more variety, you can also eat in Subic town on the mainland and then come back.

Older reviews say the island has a separate coffee shop and a restaurant near the pier, and that Filipino-style breakfast is served. Menus and prices change from year to year, so bring plenty of cash if you plan to buy food separately. If you want to fit the island in as just part of your itinerary rather than stay long, the least burdensome approach is to stay at a hotel in Subic town and cross over for just one day.
Reservations are essential. Entry to the island is arranged through the resort office, so you may be turned away if you show up on the day.
It is best to arrive at the pier at least 30–45 minutes before the boat departs.
When you book, be sure to ask whether pool use is possible and how many meals are served.
The beach and the ruin paths have little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water.
If you plan to walk the batteries and forest paths, bring sneakers, a flashlight and mosquito repellent.
You may disembark onto a floating pier, so carry a light bag and avoid slippery shoes.
Do not enter locked areas (such as Battery Warwick). Ask the staff which areas are open.
Prices and boat times change often. Check the latest announcements.
If you bring a child, ask on arrival whether life jackets are available for rent. The bottom deepens gradually, but lifeguard coverage may differ from day to day.
It is not certain that card payments are accepted, so bring some cash too. It is safest to assume there is no ATM on the island.
Grande Island is managed by a resort, so you may be refused entry without a reservation, and prices and inclusions change from year to year.
The old military structures in the forest are aged, with weak floors or overgrown areas in places, so respect safety signs and locked doors.
Reports of the island's upkeep differ greatly from source to source and year to year. Do not rely on photos alone; check recent reviews.
In the rainy season rough seas can cancel boats, so check the refund policy in advance.
The midday sun and heat are strong, so drink plenty of water.
The Subic Bay area where the island lies; you can add the parks, beaches and theme parks inside the Freeport Zone to your day. It is
15–30 minutes
away by boat.
Small islands off the Zambales coast with a lighthouse and rocky shores, a good follow-on stop for your itinerary.
A pine-fringed beach campsite in Zambales, reached by heading further north from Subic.
An airport and city area about
1 hour
from Subic by car, handy as a transport hub.
